editorial.introduction: Hyakutake passed just 0.10 AU from Earth in March 1996. Its close approach made it a striking sight despite its much smaller nucleus than Hale–Bopp’s.

selected.identity: JPL Small-Body Database designation and Horizons elements
selected.size: Radius 1.25 km, the midpoint of Harmon et al.'s 2-3 km diameter range (Harmon et al. (1997), Science 278, 1921), as the volume-equivalent radius
selected.position: Independent JPL heliocentric elements and vectors at JD2461286.5

candidateSurvey.disposition: Selected nucleus size: the midpoint of Harmon et al.'s 2-3 km radar diameter range, Science 278, 1921.
Existing scientifically reconstructed cssEarth comets are preserved. This catalog expansion does not claim a recovered mesh for new entries.

Coma, tail, spectra and encounter context are useful source material; they do not establish a nucleus surface texture. Additional quantitative shape reconstruction remains a separate source qualification.
Formerly supplied the illustrative generic mesh and a catalogue radius; retired 2026-09-16 and no longer used.

derivedFacts.perihelion: Perihelion distance q of the 1996 apparition: JPL SBDB orbit.elements.q (solution JPL 73, epoch JD2450157.5 = 1996-03-15)
derivedFacts.radius: Midpoint of Harmon et al.'s 2-3 km diameter range, Harmon et al. (1997), Science 278, 1921

assumptions: No observed albedo, mass, density, pole or placeholder rotation is imported.
No tail, coma or historical outburst is rendered.
The ellipsoid is a smooth approximation at an effective radius; no nucleus terrain measurement is claimed.

shape.convention: effective-radius-as-volume-equivalent ellipsoid; unit axis ratios unless a lightcurve ratio is cited
